title: Cross-variant weight mapping -> token index shift: incident review
body:
Summary:

On 2025-11-02 we observed a canary regression after deploying a cross-variant rollout that introduced a hybrid-quantized weight bundle for the medium-sized chat model (variant: medium-q4). Canary nodes started returning semantically incorrect tokens for a subset of inputs and alerting downstream QA/eval pipelines. The issue manifested as high generation-error rates and an increase in token-level decoding failures for non-ASCII inputs. This review captures detection, impact, root cause, mitigation steps, and recommended follow-ups.

What happened (high level):
- A staged rollout shipped a new weight bundle (medium-q4) that used a different weight-sharding ordering and an updated packaging pipeline that emits an explicit token-id remap file alongside the weights.
- The tokenizer artifact included in the release was the expected BPE vocabulary, but the packaging step that generated the mapping for the quantized embedding table sorted embedding shards in a different order than the token-to-index file (token_map.json) produced by the tokenizer build.
- On canary hosts, the runtime loaded the quantized embedding shards and applied the provided token_map, but because the ordering between shards and token_map diverged, a non-trivial set of token ids pointed to incorrect embedding vectors.
- Result: outputs for some prompts were corrupted (wrong named-entity tokens, accent/diacritic corruption, and rare token hallucinations). The fault was silent in many short tests and surfaced under the canary validation prompts used by Evals.

Detection and timeline (UTC):
- 2025-11-02 02:47: first automated canary eval job shows p95 generation-quality drop for model/medium-q4 vs baseline (0.4 -> 0.86 error rate on golden prompt set).
- 2025-11-02 03:05: SRE pager received anomaly alert: abnormal increase in token decoding errors (error_count++), and an unusual cluster of embedding similarity mismatches in the offline eval pipeline.
- 2025-11-02 03:12: on-call SRE (Daniel Park) flagged the canary instance set and started triage.
- 2025-11-02 03:28: we paused the canary rollout and suspended further region promotions.
- 2025-11-02 03:40: temporary mitigations applied: CV fallback routing to replica baseline (medium-v1) for traffic routed via the canary bucket.
- 2025-11-02 05:30: full rollback of the affected weight bundle across canary hosts completed.

Impact:
- Canary validation sets (internal) degraded for medium-q4 only; no evidence of degradation in production traffic because rollout had not reached customer-facing percentage thresholds.
- One internal automated QA job reported corrupted transcripts for a curated multi-lingual prompt set.
- No customer-facing incidents reported during this window.

Root cause (technical):
- The packaging pipeline change introduced a non-deterministic ordering step when assembling quantized embedding shards: shard files were enumerated by filesystem ordering and then concatenated. The tokenizer build step created a token_map (token -> id) file sorted by vocabulary rank. A new post-process stage attempted to create an index mapping between token_map and the concatenated shards but relied on the filesystem ordering assumption rather than consuming the model manifest ordering.
- This produced a valid-looking token_map.json that was internally consistent with the tokenizer artifact, but the embedding shard placement expected a manifest-driven order. The mismatch only appears when the packaging machine's filesystem ordering differs from the canonical manifest (happened on the build runner for the release).
- Contributing factors: lack of an explicit checksum match between tokenizer.vocab and embedding.vocab, no preflight that decodes golden prompts end-to-end after bundle assembly, and insufficient canary eval coverage for multi-lingual/rare-token prompts.

Why it was not caught earlier:
- Unit tests validated token_map and embedding sizes but did not sanity check token->embedding identity across a golden sample set.
- The CI job that runs preflight bundle checks uses a single-locale prompt bank; token-id mismatches primarily affected rare/uncommon tokens and multi-lingual diacritics which didn't exist in that bank.

Immediate mitigation actions taken:
- Paused rollout and prevented promotion of medium-q4 to additional regions.
- Rolled back canary hosts to previous stable weight bundle (medium-v1) by 05:30 UTC.
- Re-ran canary validation harness with more diverse prompt sets to confirm rollback success.
- Quarantined the offending bundle artifacts and blocked the release pipeline for that version.

Permanent fixes and follow-ups (action items):
1) (High) Packaging hardening: change bundling pipeline to use the authoritative manifest ordering when concatenating shards and emitting token_map. Add explicit checks that token_map ordering == embedding shard ordering. Owner: Sanjay Patel. ETA: 2025-11-14.
2) (High) Add end-to-end preflight: after bundle creation, run a golden prompt pass (multi-lingual + rare tokens) that compares generation outputs vs golden baseline. Fail pipeline on drift. Owner: Evelyn Zhao. ETA: 2025-11-10.
3) (Medium) CI expansion: include a randomized locale/diacritic set and coverage for tokens in the tail of the vocab. Owner: Mateo Alvarez. ETA: 2025-11-21.
4) (High) Monitoring: add a lightweight runtime check on startup that verifies tokenizer.vocab.md5 == embedding.vocab_md5 (or explicit manifest tokens checksum), and emit critical alert on mismatch. Owner: Lila Morgan. ETA: 2025-11-07.
5) (Medium) Canary eval improvement: expand canary prompt bank with explicit real-world multilingual examples and synthetic permutations to exercise rare token paths. Add a quality delta threshold gate. Owner: Daniel Park. ETA: 2025-11-14.
6) (Low) Runbook update: add a new section to the model rollout playbook to validate token->embedding parity and to include steps for immediate fallback routing. Owner: Sanjay Patel. ETA: 2025-11-12.

Post-incident retro notes (lessons learned):
- Artifact assembly assumptions are brittle — always prefer canonical manifest-driven ordering over filesystem enumeration.
- E2E checks that include a small, well-curated golden set catch semantic regressions that size/shape-only unit tests miss.
- Canary coverage must be intentionally adversarial: include multi-lingual, rare tokens, and diacritic-heavy inputs.
- Small packaging/tooling changes can have outsized user-visible effects; treat packaging code with same QA rigor as model weight transforms.

Runbook / playbook additions (concrete):
- New preflight step: "verify_token_embedding_parity" -> runs after bundle assembly; computes MD5 of tokenizer.vocab and embedding manifest token list and fails if mismatch; run on build runner.
- Canary gating: if canary eval generation-quality delta > 0.1 on golden set, auto-pause and page SRE.
- Rollback checklist: how to reroute canary bucket traffic, who to page (SRE primary + model owner), and quick sanity commands to dump the first 100 token embeddings for human inspection.

Follow-up verification performed before closing incident: 
- Rebuilt the bundle with manifest-driven ordering and re-ran the expanded canary suite (multi-lingual golden set). All checks passed.
- New startup checksum check was shipped to staging and validated against intentionally corrupted test bundles. The check raised an alert as expected.
- Packaged artifact for medium-q4 was re-promoted to canary after patch; no regressions seen in the next 48h of canary traffic.

Open items (tracking):
- Ensure all historical bundles are scanned for potential token/embedding parity issues and flag any mismatches (SRE cron job). Owner: Mateo Alvarez. ETA: 2025-11-28.
- Add a staged perturbation test to the nightly CI that intentionally permutes shard order to validate detection; adds an extra safety net. Owner: Evelyn Zhao. ETA: 2025-11-21.

Appendix (debug artifacts pointers):
- Example failing prompt (redacted): multilingual-names-with-diacritics.txt (attached internally to the JIRA).
- Canaries: canary-cluster-3a logs, bundle-checksum outputs, and packaging-runner stdout are saved in the incident ticket (ENG-4821).

Notes to self / informal observations:
- We were lucky the rollout percentage was still low; if this had slipped into wider traffic the customer impact would likely have been significant for multilingual workloads.
- Packaging runners across different datacenters show different filesystem ordering behaviors — treat that as a source of flakiness in any operation that relies on filesystem enumeration.

Prepared by: Lila Morgan (SRE)
